This is a tricky one. I kind of want to put "wait and see" but overall I think I'd hesitate to really endorse it right now. The game is fun - but, as you play, it gets worse, for the same reason so many run-based games do: you unlock so much stuff and get ZERO new ways to control what you see. My literal first 3-4 runs my choices had way more impact than any run since, because of all the reasons anyone who's seen this before can expect: * Not just "some" more stuff, but an order of magnitude more items of all types are unlocked over the course of 4-5 victories (which for me was 5-6 runs total but I've played a lot of run based games). Most of which do NOT interact with other types in a synergistic way outside of extreme edge cases * This means you basically choose your starting character, most of which come with an archtype, and lean into that from round 1. If you get unlucky, you restart in world 3 or 4 (out of 5 or 6). It's technically POSSIBLE to omega roll into broken stuff but it's so unlikely as to be even more of a waste than the run already is * Because each run is built upon "win more" shopping. The faster you win a round, the more money you get, and money is very very tight most of the time. And because the number of options the shop shows you after unlocking dozens and dozens of new items is the same as when you had NO extra unlocks, you are beholden to pure luck and rerolls - which cost money. Also, the strongest items are unsurprisingly more expensive, and you don't get much back for selling items to try and swivel and salvage a run * So that again means you pick your character at the start, hope for the right items in the first 2-3 shops (realistically), and restart if you're unlucky because you're going to get progressively less money and fewer opportunities to grow strong. Run based games with SIGNIFICANT amounts of unlocks HAVE to add a way to mitigate RNG, because otherwise they go from interesting strategic choices to build (what your first 2-3 runs here are) to pure RNG where your choice doesn't really matter because it's dictated for you - the punishments are instant and immense, and you HAVE to reach certain levels of power because each round is also RNG based anyway, excellent vocabulary will only get you so far when half your grid is A's. A lot of people in comments have asked for being able to disable items to try and mitigate the issue, which I get, but I think that's the wrong direction here - you'd have to manage that for each character or each run and it sounds tedious. What I'd rather see, and so few games try, is just... increasing the amount of choices you get. It seems obvious. You have more than doubled the pool of items, but rerolls still reroll everything, so increasing shop choices by an extra 50%-100% would increase meaningful choice a lot, and make you slightly less reliant on min-maxing economy in the first place (right now it's by far the smartest thing to go for first every run because it's fairly generic and fairly strong and the only way you can possibly take advantage of good rolls later on). So yea. I really like the gameplay. I like the builds and interactions. I just wish you got to have a say in seeing them. Some people don't care about a game literally just asking you to spend time instead of choice to win but to me, that's terrible - I want my choices to mean something in what is supposed to be a strategic genre of multipliers and bonuses and interactions. Edit: I wanted to post this as a comment but comment length is only 1,000 soooo adding it here instead, re: developer response I think the problem is, "weight" is still just RNG. It did seem there was SOME weight in my longer runs but most runs felt predetermined - maybe I just have bad luck, but at the end of the day it felt like I was just pulling a lever and seeing if I'd win, not actually making interesting choices. Because, as mentioned, the entire run is snowball based. Your first shop you get 1 free item, so you HAVE to choose one of those things or really shoot yourself in the foot. And then you can probably buy 1 more, or reroll and 1 more. So with weights, you're just building off of literally the first RNG screen you see anyway and trying to max out your early strength so you don't loose too much money so you can keep rerolling to try and get 1-2 pieces you need to be able to beat world 4 or 5 (much less 6). I saw the intent of synergies but with you having such limited control, space (you can freeze items in the shop but you can't "store" your own in case you need to revisit that build), money, and you HAVE to get such high score-multiplier combos, I saw them come to fruition like 1 time in 15 hours. You are objectively better off going with hyper-specific combined with super generic items, even if the generic ones are "weaker" at least they are going to work. Color and Cards both seem intended to work with most everything else but they also require a lot of stuff to offer meaningful score It's not that I was dreading unlocking stuff, I was intrigued by the possibilities (and I unlocked presumably a fair bit), but my actual experience the last ~8 hours of playtime was "I am not actually making any meaningful decisions in this roguelike strategy game" and it was not fun to just restart constantly. A lot of people (clearly) are fine with just being beholden to the RNG gods, and that is evident in a lot of successful RNG-is-doing-the-thinking-for-you games that have done well, but it's boring and frustrating to me. I don't need every run to be winnable but I need most runs to be lost because of MY decisions and skills, rather than what the game decided, and that's just not my experience here. Weighted dice are still dice and the game is SO unforgiving once you unlock stuff and get past the tutorial difficulties, there isn't much wiggle room for strategy in the first place (but there is some, in the theoretical world where you get real choices), much less with the RNG dictating everything for you. To me, it just makes the game "solved". The choices are always objectively correct or incorrect, because you get so few of them, and the requirements are strict enough that sub-par ones become wrong. The question becomes do the dice allow you to win or not rather than does MY knowledge allow me to win or not.

Clever setup but whereas Balatro often caused you to say "Wow, I didn't realize my buffs would react that way! Cool!" this game frequently made me say "Wait, why didn't that trigger a buff. Why did this work on Grid 1 but not 3? Wait, that counted as cursed last round but not this one?" There's major inconsistencies in how the stamps/stickers work and the game is extremely bad at explaining what's going on. The real problem is that unlike Balatro, each run generates a TON of cognitive load because you're not building from a small amount of legal hands, you're drawing from every word that exists (in multiple languages). This makes every round take forever (and i know the gimmick is that you're stacking wildcards but you still have to think through basic word construction each time). This leads to runs that feel looooong and unsatisfying when the difficulty ramps. In Balatro you can kind of bop through antes and if your hand sucks, you figure it out fast and can reload. In this game, your runs are often doomed way before you realize it leading to the feeling that you wasted time you should've spent reloading. I dunno, there's some decent stuff here but it's clunky, uneven, and inconsistent. They traded clarity for ~quirky mystery~ and I think that was a huge blunder because their systems are not tight at all.

Cursed Words is an absolute fever dream of a game that starts out as Balatro but for Boggle. You get a grid with letters in it and make words using straight or diagonal lines (or some combination thereof). For the first two runs, you're mostly running entirely on luck. Then you unlock the third character, and all hell breaks loose. Suddenly, 1234AY789 is a word. So is 1/3 2/8 3/7 4/8 5/10. So is a long string of random chess notation. The game starts throwing points at you for reasons you barely understand, and soon you've won the state Boggle championships by walking in, throwing your chair at the judge, giving your opponent both middle fingers and counting to ten. The game stops being about making words and starts becoming a game about breaking the game the way Balatro is. This game is absolutely worth the money.

A wordsearch roguelike sounds like a really fun idea. Introducing unique concepts like numbers that substitute any letter or chess mechanics sounds like a really fun idea. Unfortunately, you cannot do both. The moment you start unlocking all the characters and items, the game stops requiring you to think and try to form words and becomes a mindless slog of how many 'cursed' tiles can I link together to form a 19 letter word you've never heard of. It's a shame, I wanted to like this.

1XQ4$♘♛⅞ See that? That spells "EXQUISITE." Heck of a Scrabble word, that - the Q and the X of Spades are both worth quite a bit. Oh, plus my knight captured the white queen, so that's another 12 points. But oh shoot, I could've used a Joker instead of that dollar sign to give myself a flush! Welcome to Cursed Words, where Balatro meets Boggle. Things start innocently enough, the game tasking you with putting together words by connecting tiles in a grid. Each letter is worth a couple of points, and if you collect enough points over the course of 5 grids, you move on to the next level. Even when you start buying powerups in the shop, it's very straightforward: add a few blue tiles to the grid; blue tiles are worth more points; turn some of those blue tiles into ? wildcards. Easy! Then come the numbers. Then card suits. Negative tiles. Fractions. Chess pieces. Currency. Next thing you know, you're spelling T2⅓♜J?₩?9♦ and the game is saying that you submitted TOMAHAWKED for 5600 points. It makes no sense. But it makes so much sense at the same time. If you enjoy the "big numbers go brrr" combos of Balatro and want a fresh twist on the format, and maybe if you like feeling absolutely insane, look no further.

Actually a very solid and original roguelike crossword/word search puzzle in the spirit of Balatro. Significantly underrated, a bit on the easy side outside of challenges, but very fun nonetheless. The game does requires English fluency at minimum to be played properly, which is probably part of its lower player/review count. There is also Spanish, German and French languages, but they are not the intended experience and will likely have balance and functionality issues. By design the game does not punish you for not having an extensive vocabulary as you can just try combinations until you have a valid word, although linguistic skills ARE rewarded. The way the game evolves as you unlock more content is really cool and interesting, it adds a lot to the gameplay and quickly becomes amusing chaos where it's less about words or letters, and more about a monstrous amalgation of several table games, while never fully losing the word game aspect. Just don't expect it to remain some kind of tame scrabble. Some people will complain about diluted pools, but that is a rather asinine criticism as the game feels way more balanced when it has more content, and games are meant to get harder the futher you progress through them, aren't they? The game feels how it should feel when the pool is bigger. The early game state is the game with the training wheels on, not understanding that is having it backward. Otherwise there are already some very abusable strategies that become way too consistent compared to others. Some people expect that out of a roguelike, that's missing the entire point of the genre. And even then there are a few items that help with the economy/rerolls, very generous shop refreshes on top of the shop having a bias for items that fit your build, which at that point if you still have an issue with the item pool... it's either a skill issue or the RNG gods having it out for you, sorry.

The year is not over yet, but I already know my 2026 GOTY: a roguelike word game that uses a very loose definition of "word". This game is simply full of joy and was clearly made with lots of care. The cartoony character design is delightful and there's just so much content - I feel like the devs could have released this game with half as much of everything and it would still be great - but they still gave us multiple characters to unlock (each one of them with their own, often pretty crazy, gimmick), plenty of challenges, a ton of stickers and stamps that let you create endless fun builds and synergies, and also some secrets to discover. And there's no unnecessary handholding - you just organically discover how things work. This is the first time since my childhood that I've experienced so much sense of wonder while playing a video game. This review is kinda sappy (sorry!) but I assure you that the game isn't - it's creative and hilarious. Go and create some cursed words, you won't regret it. At the time of me writing this review Cursed Words has a free demo available - I really recommend checking it out. It's quite long... but it still ends before things get really crazy :)

Absolutely stellar little game. Make no mistake, the title isn't lying. Having a big vocabulary doesn't hurt, for sure, but the game very quickly becomes about how fast you can stop spelling words and start counting. Or playing chess. Or mahjong, apparently, haven't unlocked that one yet. It's taking more than its fair share from Balatro; this is a game won in the shop as much as it is on the board. It altogether manages to tickle a different part of my brain though, and more than stands tall as it's own thing. The experience is rounded out by a soundscape with a charming amount of detail put in. Tiles make clacking noises if they're letters, like the noises scrabble tiles would, but change to cards being pulled from a deck if they're suited (don't worry about it), certain upgrades can add instruments to the soundtrack, and so on. Runs like a dream, in my experience. Definitely worth picking up on any kind of sale, but more than worth considering at full price.
